summary: Applied vocabulary for wave behaviour (reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, amplitude, wavelength, frequency, echo, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection) for ages 9–11. The teaching goal is precise, applied USE of a highly confusable term set, not rote definition: each word is taught against its nearest confusable neighbour on a single discriminator, and every term is immediately used to explain a real phenomenon (bent straw = refraction, echo = reflected sound, blue sky = scattering, prism = spectrum). Core discriminator: does the wave bounce back into the first medium (reflection), pass into a new medium and change direction at the boundary when it meets it at an angle (refraction), get sent off in many directions by a rough surface or by tiny particles such as those in air (scattering), or soak in and not return (absorption)? The three wave-property words pin to distinct features of one wave — amplitude = height from the middle (rest) line to a peak, wavelength = peak-to-peak distance, frequency = how many pass per second.
misconceptions: Swapping reflection and refraction — treating light that crosses into a new medium (refraction) as if it bounces off it (reflection).
Believing reflection is 'only mirrors' and refraction is 'only glass blocks', rather than every surface reflecting and any change of medium refracting.
Reading 'bending' (refraction) as light travelling in a CURVE instead of a change from one straight-line path to another.
Measuring the angle of incidence/reflection from the SURFACE rather than from the normal (the perpendicular).
Blurring amplitude, wavelength and frequency into a vague single 'size' of the wave instead of three distinct measurable features.
Not recognising absorption as an option (forcing every light–surface interaction into reflect or refract), and confusing scattering with plain mirror-like reflection.
Treating an 'echo' as a mysterious separate effect rather than simply reflected sound.

activities.title: One ray, four fates: send a ray at a boundary
steps: Send a single light ray at a surface at an angle (not straight along the normal) and change what the surface is: a mirror, a block of glass or water, black card, and a rough/bumpy surface.

Watch and name the main outcome each time: mirror = bounces back off the surface (reflection); glass or water = most of the light passes through and bends at the surface (refraction), though a little is also reflected; black card = most of the light is soaked in and not returned (absorption); rough surface = sprays off in many directions (scattering).

Keep the SAME incoming ray and switch the surface from glass to mirror, and describe out loud how the ray changes from refracting to reflecting — the two most-confused words are two different fates of one ray.
Trace or draw the bent ray for refraction as two straight segments with a kink at the surface, NOT a curve.
State the first medium each time (usually air) and say which medium the ray crosses into.
activities.insight: Reflection, refraction, absorption and scattering are different things a wave can do when it meets a boundary; reflection (bounce back) and refraction (pass through and bend) are distinguished by whether the wave enters the new medium. Refraction is a change from one straight path to another with a kink at the boundary, not a curve.

activities.title: Measuring angles from the normal
steps: On a reflection diagram, draw the normal — the line perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray hits.
Measure the angle of incidence between the incoming ray and the normal, and the angle of reflection between the outgoing ray and the normal (for example with a protractor aligned to the normal).
Check that the two angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface, and compare them.
State in words: the angle of incidence and angle of reflection are both measured from the normal (the perpendicular).
activities.insight: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal (the perpendicular to the surface), never from the surface itself.

activities.title: One wave, three features: amplitude, wavelength, frequency
steps: Look at a single labelled wave and identify amplitude = height, wavelength = distance from one peak to the next, frequency = how many waves pass per second.

Change one control at a time (for example an amplitude control, then a frequency control) and describe which feature changed and which word names it; notice that changing the amplitude leaves the peak spacing alone, but for a wave in the same material, raising the frequency makes the peaks closer together (shorter wavelength).
Say aloud a one-line distinction for each so they don't blur into a single vague 'size': amplitude is how tall, wavelength is how far apart the peaks are, frequency is how many per second.
Connect to sound: loudness/volume links to amplitude (size of the vibration) and pitch links to frequency (how fast it vibrates).
activities.insight: Amplitude, wavelength and frequency are three distinct, separately measurable features of one wave, not interchangeable words for its overall 'size'.

activities.title: Use the word to explain the phenomenon
steps: For each everyday scene, say which term applies and why, in a full sentence: a straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water (refraction); you shout in a tunnel and hear your voice come back (echo — reflected sound); the sky looks blue (scattering); a prism makes a rainbow (spectrum).
Explain an echo as reflected sound, linking it to the same 'bounce off a surface' idea as light reflection (like seeing yourself in a mirror).

Explain the dull red jumper in shade: it absorbs most colours and reflects/scatters red, and in shade there is less light to reflect, so it looks duller (an illustrative case that depends on the actual material and lighting).
Sort a mix of scenarios into reflect / refract / absorb / scatter and justify each choice.
Use word-part cues to spell and separate the tricky pair: re-FLECT = bounce back, re-FRACT = break/bend through, ab-SORB = soak in.
activities.insight: Each wave term earns its keep by explaining a real phenomenon; mastery is applying the right word in context, keeping reflection distinct from refraction, and recognising an echo as simply reflected sound.

checkQuestion: Here are three things happening: a straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water; you shout in a tunnel and hear your voice come back a moment later; and a red jumper looks dull in the shade. Tell me what's happening in each, using the right wave words — you might need reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, echo. Explain your choices.
checkAnswer: The bent straw = refraction (light changes direction and speed crossing the water-air boundary). The voice coming back = an echo, which is reflection of sound off the tunnel wall. The dull red jumper = it absorbs most colours and reflects/scatters red, and in shade there is less light to reflect. Terms are USED correctly and reflection is kept distinct from refraction.
